questions.stem: A new supervisor at a parish tax office wants to monitor her team's work fairly. What should she make sure of first?
options: That each officer knows she will check their work daily
That the team's overtime has been approved for the year
That each officer knows the standards and targets expected
That every officer's past appraisal scores are on her desk

options: File all incoming letters within two working days
Try much harder to keep the filing room in good order
Do as much filing as possible each week when time allows

options: Agreed targets can be changed by officers at any time they like
Agreed targets remove the need for the manager to check the work
Agreed targets are never linked to the agency's corporate plan
Officers are more committed to targets they helped to shape

questions.stem: In a public agency, what is a performance standard?
options: A list of the duties set out in a person's job description
A stated level of quality, quantity or time for a task
A record of the training an officer has completed
The salary scale that applies to a grade of post

questions.stem: Which is a key performance indicator (KPI) for a passport office's customer counter?

The colour scheme of the customer waiting area

options: Soon after the work, while it is fresh in mind

options: Goal, Reality, Options, Way forward
Guide, Review, Order, Warn

questions.stem: What is the main difference between coaching and telling an officer what to do?
options: Coaching is only ever done by people brought in from outside the agency
Coaching is a formal step in the discipline procedure

questions.stem: Why should a manager keep a brief record of feedback meetings with each officer?
options: So the record can be shown to the rest of the team
So progress can be tracked and the facts are clear later

So the manager does not need to hold the appraisal

questions.stem: Which is the most suitable way to store notes about officers' performance?
options: On a shared drive that all staff can open and read
In a folder on the front desk for easy access
In the manager's personal email account at home
Securely, with access limited to those who need it

questions.stem: What should a manager write in a note of a feedback meeting?
options: Personal views about the officer's character and home life
Facts discussed, the officer's views and the actions agreed
Only the points on which the manager and officer disagreed
Comments that other staff made about the officer in private

questions.stem: A tax office team misses its monthly target for the third time. Monitoring shows each officer is busy but files wait days between steps. What is the most likely cause to look at?
options: The personal effort of each officer in the team
The way work flows between the steps of the process

options: To shame the members who are doing the least work in the team
To replace one-to-one feedback with the officers
To meet a rule that every figure must be on the wall
To help the team see progress and solve problems together

options: A short anonymous survey after each service

Asking only the customers who praise the team

questions.stem: In 360-degree feedback, who gives views on a manager's performance?
options: Only the manager's own line manager
Only members of the public who are served
Managers, peers, staff and sometimes clients

questions.stem: A senior officer tells the unit head that her instructions are often unclear. How should the unit head respond?
options: Explain that senior staff should understand her
Thank him, ask for examples and agree a change

options: So the manager does not have to prepare for it

options: Explain the colleague's problems so he understands

options: It is unfair treatment that may break the law and public service rules

options: Insist the forms are done exactly as before

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: Give the five-letter word used to describe targets that are specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.
Give the three-letter abbreviation for a measure used to track progress towards an important target.
An officer at a public agency dealt with 171 of 190 requests within the target time. What percentage met the target?
Four applications took 3, 5, 9 and 7 working days to process. What was the average, in working days?
What two-word name is given to the rating error in which one strong good point colours the whole rating?
What two-word name is given to the rating error in which recent events outweigh the rest of the review period?
What term describes the habit of giving everyone a middle rating to avoid high or low scores?
Give the three-letter abbreviation for the feedback model that describes the situation, the behaviour and its impact.
Name the four-letter coaching model whose stages are Goal, Reality, Options and Way forward.
What name is given to feedback on a person's work collected from their manager, peers, staff and sometimes clients?
What is the term for an officer's own review of their performance, written before a review meeting?

essays.stem: You have just become supervisor of a team of eight officers who process benefit applications at a government agency in May Pen. Plan how you will monitor the team's performance over the next six months.
essays.modelAnswer: I would begin by checking the agency's corporate plan and the unit's work plan, so the team's work links to the agency's goals. In the first two weeks I would meet each officer to agree their duties, standards and targets, such as processing 95% of applications within ten working days with no more than 2% returned for errors. I would collect a baseline from the past three months' records so later results can be compared fairly. I would then choose a small set of measures: volume, time taken, error rate and client feedback. Data would come from the case system, a weekly sample check of five files per officer, and a short client survey. I would hold a monthly one-to-one with each officer and a short weekly team huddle to look at the figures together. I would keep dated notes for each officer, stored securely. After three months I would review whether the measures are useful and fair, and change them with the team if needed, before the six-month review.
markingPoints: Links the team's targets to the agency's plans and agrees them with each officer
Takes a baseline and sets a small set of balanced measures (volume, time, quality, feedback)
Uses several sources of evidence, such as system data, file checks and client feedback
Plans a routine of one-to-ones and team reviews, with secure dated notes
Reviews the monitoring system itself and adjusts it with the team

essays.stem: Tanisha Campbell, an officer in a municipal corporation's planning department, has submitted three site reports late this month and one had wrong measurements. Describe how you would plan and hold a feedback meeting with her.
essays.modelAnswer: Before the meeting I would check the facts: the dates the reports were due and submitted, the error in the measurements and its effect, for example a delayed approval. I would also look at what she does well, so the feedback is balanced. I would book a private room and enough time, and tell her the purpose in advance. In the meeting I would start by explaining why we are meeting, then describe each problem using the situation-behaviour-impact approach: for example, the Old Harbour report was due on the 5th, came in on the 12th, and the applicant had to wait a week. I would then ask for her view and listen carefully, as there may be causes such as workload, transport to sites or unclear instructions. Together we would agree actions: perhaps a site visit schedule, a measurement check with a colleague, and weekly progress checks. I would also mention what she does well. Afterwards I would write a brief note of the facts and agreed actions, give her a copy, and follow up on the date we set.
markingPoints: Prepares by checking facts and dates, and notes strengths as well
Holds the meeting privately and explains its purpose
Describes specific behaviour and its impact rather than personal traits
Asks for her view, listens and explores the causes
Agrees actions and support, records them and follows up

essays.stem: Explain the common errors managers make when judging staff performance, and recommend how a public agency can reduce them.
essays.modelAnswer: Several errors can make performance judgements unfair. The halo effect happens when one strong point, such as good public speaking, leads the manager to rate everything highly; the horns effect is the opposite. The recency effect gives too much weight to the last few weeks. Central tendency means rating everyone in the middle to avoid hard conversations, while leniency or strictness means rating everyone too high or too low. There is also bias based on liking, similarity, or personal characteristics such as religion, gender or age, which is unfair and may break the law and public service rules. To reduce these errors, the agency should judge staff against clear, agreed standards and targets, and use several sources of evidence, such as system data, file checks and client feedback. Managers should keep dated notes through the year rather than relying on memory. Training for managers on rating errors helps them spot their own habits. A second-level review of ratings by a senior manager, and comparing ratings across units, can show patterns of unfairness. Officers should also be able to comment on their review.
markingPoints: Explains the halo (or horns) effect
Explains the recency effect and central tendency or leniency
Explains personal bias and that unfair treatment may break the law and public service rules
Recommends clear standards, several sources of evidence and dated notes
Recommends manager training, second-level review or the officer's right to comment

essays.stem: Compare formal and informal feedback in the workplace, and explain how a manager in a public body should use each.
essays.modelAnswer: Informal feedback is given during normal work, often on the spot: a quick word of praise after a good client meeting, or a short private comment when a form is filled in wrongly. It is timely, simple and keeps small problems small. Its weakness is that it may be forgotten and is not usually recorded, so it may not count later. Formal feedback is planned and recorded. It happens in scheduled one-to-ones, mid-year and yearly reviews, and in improvement plans. It looks at performance over a longer period against agreed targets, gives both sides time to prepare, and leaves a record for development and decisions. Its weaknesses are that it takes more time and, if it is the only feedback, comes too late to help. A manager in a public body should use both. Informal feedback should be frequent and specific, so officers always know how they are doing. Formal meetings should bring the evidence together, agree goals and record actions. Nothing said at a formal review should be a surprise, because it should already have been raised informally.
markingPoints: Describes informal feedback and its strengths (timely, simple)
Notes the weakness of informal feedback (not recorded, may be forgotten)
Describes formal feedback and its strengths (planned, evidence-based, recorded)
Notes the weakness of formal feedback (time, can come too late)
Recommends using both, so that a formal review holds no surprises

essays.stem: A ministry unit has a new dashboard showing each officer's cases closed, average time and complaints. Evaluate the benefits and limits of using it to monitor performance.
essays.modelAnswer: The dashboard has clear benefits. It gives up-to-date, objective figures, so the manager can see trends quickly and spot problems such as a growing backlog before they become serious. Officers can see their own progress, which can motivate them, and the figures give a factual basis for feedback and reduce the risk of bias from memory or personal liking. It also saves the time of collecting figures by hand. However, it has limits. Numbers show what happened, not why: an officer with fewer cases closed may be dealing with the hardest ones. A focus on speed can push staff to rush and cut quality. Complaints may reflect the type of client rather than the officer's work. Some important work, such as helping colleagues or advising the public by phone, may not appear at all. The data may also contain errors. I would recommend using the dashboard as a starting point for conversations, checking the data, adding quality measures such as file checks and client feedback, and never judging an officer on the figures alone.
markingPoints: Explains benefits: timely, objective data and early warning of problems
Explains benefits for officers and for fair, factual feedback
Explains that figures show what, not why, and may hide case difficulty
Explains risks of rushing, missing work and data errors
Recommends using the dashboard with quality checks and conversation, not alone

essays.stem: Monitoring shows that an experienced clerk in a parish court office, who used to be reliable, is now making frequent errors. Describe the steps you would take, from first noticing the problem to deciding whether formal action is needed.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would check the evidence: which errors, how often, since when, and whether the data is correct. Because the clerk used to be reliable, I would look for a change, such as a new system, a heavier workload or a personal difficulty. I would then meet the clerk privately, describe the facts calmly and ask open questions to understand what has changed. If the cause is personal, such as illness or family stress, I would show concern and point the clerk to support such as the employee assistance service, while keeping the matter confidential. If the cause is work-related, such as a new case system, I would arrange training or coaching, or adjust the workload. We would agree a short improvement plan with clear actions, support, dates and how progress will be checked, and I would record it. I would monitor progress and give regular, balanced feedback, including praise when things improve. Only if there is no real improvement after fair support and time would I take advice from the human resource unit and follow the agency's formal procedure.
markingPoints: Checks the evidence and looks for what has changed
Meets privately, states facts and asks open questions about causes
Responds to personal causes with support and confidentiality
Uses training, coaching or workload changes and agrees a recorded improvement plan
Monitors with feedback and uses the formal procedure, with HR advice, only if support fails

essays.stem: Explain why recognising good performance matters in a public body, and describe ways a manager can do it when there is little money for rewards.
essays.modelAnswer: Recognition tells officers that their effort is seen and valued. It reinforces good behaviour, so it is more likely to be repeated, and it shows the rest of the team what good work looks like. It also lifts morale and helps keep good staff, which matters in the public sector where pay is set by grade and cannot easily be raised for one person. When money is short, a manager can still recognise good work in many ways. Specific, sincere praise given soon after the event is the simplest: for example, thanking an officer for calming an upset client and explaining what she did well. Praise can be given in front of the team or written in a note copied to a senior manager. Good work can be featured in the agency's newsletter or at a staff meeting. Officers can be given more interesting work, the chance to lead a project, to train others or to attend a course. Good performance should also be recorded in the appraisal. Recognition must be fair and based on evidence, so it does not look like favouritism.
markingPoints: Explains that recognition reinforces good behaviour and sets an example
Explains effects on morale and keeping staff, especially where pay is fixed
Describes specific, timely praise, in person or in writing
Describes non-money rewards such as newsletter mentions, new tasks, training or leading projects
Notes that recognition must be fair, evidence-based and recorded

essays.stem: A statutory body plans to use 360-degree feedback for its middle managers. Evaluate this plan and recommend how it should be introduced.
essays.modelAnswer: 360-degree feedback collects views on a manager from their own manager, peers, the staff they lead and sometimes clients. Its strengths are that it gives a fuller picture than one person's view, shows managers how their behaviour affects others, and often reveals blind spots, such as poor listening, that a line manager never sees. It can support development and make leadership more open. The risks are that staff may fear giving honest views about their boss, that some may use it to settle scores, and that results can hurt if delivered badly. It also takes time to run, and if it is tied to pay or promotion, people may rate tactically. I would recommend using it for development rather than for pay decisions at first. The body should explain the purpose clearly, use a short questionnaire on agreed management behaviours, keep answers anonymous with a minimum number of raters, and store results securely. Each manager should receive results in a private meeting with a trained person and agree a development plan. The scheme should be piloted and reviewed after a year.
markingPoints: Explains what 360-degree feedback is
Evaluates strengths: fuller picture, blind spots, development
Evaluates risks: fear, score-settling, harm from poor delivery, tactical rating
Recommends development use, clear purpose, anonymity and secure records
Recommends a trained person to give results, a development plan and a pilot

essays.stem: A Kingston government records office is missing its targets for responding to requests from the public. Plan how you would use monitoring and feedback to improve the whole team's performance.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start by gathering facts: the number of requests each week, how long each takes, where requests wait, and the main reasons for delay, using the case log and a sample of files. I would share the figures openly with the team at a meeting and ask for their ideas, as the staff often know what slows the work, such as a missing form or a single officer who must sign everything. Together we would agree a few clear team measures, such as the share of requests answered within ten working days and the backlog at the end of each week, and display them where everyone can see them. I would hold a short weekly huddle to look at the figures, celebrate progress and solve problems. Alongside this, I would give individual feedback in one-to-ones, recognising officers who improve and supporting those who struggle with coaching or training. I would also ask a sample of the public for feedback. After three months I would review the results, keep what works and change what does not.
markingPoints: Gathers data on volumes, times and causes of delay
Shares data openly and involves the team in finding causes and solutions
Agrees clear team measures and makes them visible
Uses regular team reviews and individual feedback, praise and support
Seeks public feedback and reviews results after a set period

essays.stem: Explain why a manager should seek feedback on their own performance from the team, and describe how to ask for it and respond to it.
essays.modelAnswer: Managers often do not see how their own behaviour affects others. Asking the team for feedback helps a manager find blind spots, such as unclear instructions or late decisions, and improve. It also shows the team that feedback is normal and two-way, which builds trust and makes officers more open to the manager's feedback in return. To ask for it, the manager should make it safe and easy. She might ask specific questions at the end of a one-to-one, such as "What is one thing I could do differently to help you?", or use a short anonymous survey, since some staff will not speak openly to their boss. She could also invite views in a team review. When feedback comes, she should listen without arguing, thank the person, and ask for examples if the point is unclear. She should not try to find out who said what in an anonymous survey. She should then choose one or two changes, tell the team what she will do, act on it, and later ask whether the change has helped. Doing nothing after asking will damage trust.
markingPoints: Explains that it reveals blind spots and helps the manager improve
Explains that it builds trust and models two-way feedback
Describes safe ways to ask, such as specific questions or an anonymous survey
Describes responding well: listen, thank, ask for examples, no blame
Describes acting on it, reporting back and checking later

practical1.title: Build a monitoring plan and analyse a month of team performance data
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a case about a made-up public service team (for example the licensing unit of a municipal corporation) with its targets and a spreadsheet of one month's work for six officers: cases received, cases closed, days taken, errors found in file checks and client comments. As a group, prepare a monitoring plan and a short performance report for the unit head. Give each member a named role: planning lead (writes the monitoring plan: measures, sources of evidence, timetable and who does what), data analyst (works out each officer's and the team's results against target in the spreadsheet, checking every figure twice), quality checker (reviews the error and client comment data and notes what the figures do not show), report writer (writes a one-page report with findings, possible causes and recommendations), and presenter (presents the findings to the assessor in 10 minutes, with help from the others). In a group of four, the planning lead also presents. Use made-up officer names only and keep the report factual and fair.
materials: Case brief and team data spreadsheet from the assessor
Computers with spreadsheet and word processor software
photos: The written monitoring plan with measures, evidence and timetable
The spreadsheet on screen with results against target for each officer and the team
A chart of the team's results
The quality checker's notes on what the figures do not show
The one-page performance report and the group presenting it
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the work
Monitoring plan links measures to the team's targets and uses more than one source of evidence
Percentages, averages and gaps against target are correct and were checked twice
Notes the limits of the data and avoids judging officers on figures alone
Report gives fair, factual findings, likely causes and practical recommendations
Presented clearly and answered the assessor's questions
safety: Treat the case data as confidential staff information; hand all printouts to the assessor at the end
Use made-up names only and write about performance, not about people's character
Respect each other's views; disagree with ideas, not people
Share the workload fairly and take a short break

practical2.title: Role-play feedback conversations and record the agreed actions
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group three short cases from a made-up public body (for example a ministry's records unit): an officer who has done excellent work, an officer whose reports are late, and an officer who becomes defensive when given feedback. As a group, plan and role-play a feedback meeting for each case, then a fourth meeting in which a manager asks the team for feedback on her own leadership. Each member has a named role in each round, and the roles rotate so that every member gives feedback at least once: manager (prepares and leads the meeting), officer (plays the role card from the assessor), note-taker (records the facts discussed, the officer's views and the actions agreed), and observer (scores the meeting on a checklist: facts, behaviour and impact, listening, agreed actions, tone). In a group of five, the fifth member acts as timekeeper and second observer. Each meeting lasts 10 to 12 minutes. After each round the observer gives brief feedback, and the manager writes up a short meeting note with the agreed actions and a follow-up date.
materials: Case cards and role cards from the assessor
Feedback meeting planning sheet and observer checklist templates
